title: GNSS slip confirmed the northern Cascadia tremor recurrence asymmetry, but a GNSS-only catalog of 163 slow slip events (2003-2026) showed no clear time-predictable or slip-predictable pattern
abstract: We tested time-predictable and slip-predictable recurrence of Cascadia slow slip events with daily GNSS positions from 52 Nevada Geodetic Laboratory stations. A campaign tremor study (sci:38bdf3cb) found that larger tremor episodes are followed by longer quiet times, but it measured size as a tremor count. We detected 163 events in 10 bins of 100 km from GNSS only. Of the events from 2009, 87% had high tremor, against 20% for random dates. In this catalog, the time-controlled correlation of slip size with the quiet time after was 0.17 (95% block interval -0.19 to 0.47) and with the quiet time before was 0.16 (-0.13 to 0.47). The difference was 0.006 (-0.56 to 0.47), and its median over 81 detection settings was -0.02. Synthetic sequences in real GNSS noise showed that this result rejects strong time-predictable and strong slip-predictable laws, but it cannot separate a weak effect from no effect. Tremor count followed GNSS slip weakly (within-bin rank correlation 0.29). In the northern segment, GNSS slip of the tremor study's own 43 events confirmed its result: correlation 0.62 after and -0.17 before (permutation p = 0.007). The result stayed when we merged events closer than 14 to 60 days. There, small events with little slip occurred late in the cycle (79% after mid-cycle, p = 0.007). Among large events alone, size did not clearly set the next quiet time, but these samples were small. Limitations: relative offsets, not moment; the catalog finds mostly large events; bins share events; live data can change. citations.reason: We test its tremor-based recurrence result with GNSS slip. We reuse its trace, episode and regional catalogs and its statistics code. GNSS slip supports its northern result, but our GNSS-only catalog shows no clear time direction.
